disease.name: Urinary Tract Infection
disease.scientific_name: Cystitis / Acute Lower Urinary Tract Infection

overview.description: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI), particularly cystitis, is an infection and inflammation of the bladder and lower urinary tract, most commonly caused by bacterial pathogens ascending from the periurethral area. Escherichia coli accounts for 75-95% of uncomplicated cases. It is one of the most common bacterial infections in humans, especially women, due to anatomical factors (short urethra close to anus). Symptoms include dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. While uncomplicated cases respond well to short-course antibiotics, complicated UTIs, recurrent infections, and upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) can lead to significant morbidity including sepsis.
overview.affected_organ: Urinary Bladder and Urethra (Lower Urinary Tract); can ascend to ureters and kidneys (pyelonephritis)
overview.prevalence: Extremely common; lifetime risk approximately 50% in women. Accounts for over 8.6 million ambulatory care visits annually in the US. Annual incidence around 10% in women.
overview.age_group: Peak incidence in young sexually active women (18-24 years); also highly prevalent in postmenopausal women and elderly of both sexes.

anatomy_and_physiology.urinary_tract: The urinary tract includes kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. Lower UTI primarily affects the bladder (cystitis). The female urethra is short (3-4 cm) and located near the anus and vagina, facilitating bacterial entry from intestinal flora.
anatomy_and_physiology.normal_defenses: Continuous urine flow (hydrokinetic defense), glycosaminoglycan layer on urothelium, Tamm-Horsfall protein, secretory IgA, acidic vaginal pH maintained by lactobacilli, and innate immune responses.
anatomy_and_physiology.why_women_more_susceptible: Short urethra, proximity to anus and vagina, sexual intercourse (mechanical introduction of bacteria), spermicides disrupting normal flora, and postmenopausal estrogen deficiency leading to atrophic changes.
anatomy_and_physiology.mcburney_equivalent: Suprapubic tenderness is the hallmark physical finding in cystitis, analogous to McBurney's point in appendicitis.

types.name: Uncomplicated Cystitis
types.description: Acute bacterial infection of the bladder in otherwise healthy, non-pregnant, premenopausal women without structural or functional urinary tract abnormalities.
types.pathology: Bacterial invasion of bladder mucosa causing inflammation without upper tract involvement
types.prognosis: Excellent with prompt treatment; low complication rate

types.name: Complicated UTI
types.description: UTI occurring in the presence of risk factors that increase the chance of therapeutic failure, recurrence, or serious complications.
types.common_in: Men, pregnant women, elderly, diabetics, patients with catheters, stones, or obstruction
types.pathology: Often involves resistant organisms or impaired host defenses
types.management: Longer antibiotic courses (7-14 days), culture-guided therapy, investigation of underlying cause
types.prognosis: Guarded; higher risk of progression to pyelonephritis or sepsis

types.name: Recurrent UTI
types.description: Two or more episodes within 6 months or three or more within 12 months.
types.management: Prophylaxis (antibiotic or non-antibiotic), behavioral modifications, investigation for underlying abnormalities

types.name: Catheter-Associated UTI (CAUTI)
types.description: UTI in patients with indwelling urinary catheters, often biofilm-related.
types.common_in: Hospitalized and long-term care facility residents
types.pathology: Biofilm formation on catheter surface by uropathogens
types.prognosis: Higher morbidity; prevention through catheter care bundles is critical

types.name: Acute Pyelonephritis
types.description: Upper UTI involving the kidneys, usually ascending from cystitis.
types.pathology: Renal parenchymal inflammation, possible abscess formation
types.management: IV antibiotics initially, hospitalization in severe cases
types.prognosis: Good with timely treatment; risk of renal scarring if recurrent

severity_levels.name: Mild Uncomplicated Cystitis
severity_levels.description: Isolated lower urinary symptoms without fever or systemic involvement.
severity_levels.clinical_features: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic tenderness; no fever

severity_levels.name: Moderate UTI
severity_levels.description: Severe local symptoms or mild systemic features.
severity_levels.clinical_features: Gross hematuria, significant discomfort, low-grade fever

severity_levels.name: Severe / Complicated UTI or Pyelonephritis
severity_levels.description: Systemic involvement or presence of complicating factors.
severity_levels.clinical_features: Fever >38°C, flank pain, nausea, vomiting, hemodynamic instability
severity_levels.management: Hospitalization, IV antibiotics, source control if needed

causes.primary_cause: Bacterial infection, most commonly ascending from the periurethral region.
most_common_pathogens: Klebsiella pneumoniae, Proteus mirabilis, Enterococcus faecalis
pathophysiological_sequence: Periurethral colonization by fecal or vaginal flora
Adherence to uroepithelial cells via bacterial adhesins (fimbriae)
Ascension into bladder facilitated by short female urethra
Colonization and biofilm formation in bladder
Invasion of mucosa causing inflammation and symptoms
In complicated cases: impaired clearance or host defenses allow deeper invasion or persistence
risk_factors: Urinary tract obstruction, stones, or anatomical abnormalities
genetic_factors: Genetic variations affecting bacterial adherence receptors or immune response

primary_symptoms.name: Dysuria
primary_symptoms.description: Burning, stinging, or pain during urination — the hallmark symptom.

primary_symptoms.name: Urinary Frequency
primary_symptoms.description: Increased frequency of urination, often small volumes.

warning_signs_of_attack: Flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness (pyelonephritis)
Nausea, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral intake
Confusion or altered mental status (especially elderly)
symptoms_in_children: Fever, irritability, vomiting, poor feeding or appetite
New onset bedwetting in a previously continent child
symptoms_in_elderly: Delirium, confusion, falls, or functional decline
symptoms_in_pregnancy: Same as non-pregnant but higher risk of rapid progression to pyelonephritis

physical_examination_signs.costovertebral_angle_tenderness: Flank tenderness suggesting upper tract involvement

risk_factors: Urinary tract obstruction, stones, or anatomical abnormalities

physical_examination: Flank examination for costovertebral angle tenderness

clinical_scoring_systems.components: Dysuria + frequency without vaginal discharge has high positive predictive value (~90%)

diagnostic_tests.purpose: Gold standard for diagnosis and guiding therapy in complicated cases

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in women of reproductive age.

medications.note: All medications should be taken only under the supervision of a licensed physician. Antibiotic selection must consider local resistance patterns, patient factors, and culture results when available.

categories.purpose: Short-course therapy with minimal ecological impact

medicines.name: Nitrofurantoin
side_effects: Nausea, headache, rare pulmonary toxicity with long-term use

medicines.name: Trimethoprim/Sulfamethoxazole
medicines.use_case: Effective when local resistance is low

categories.purpose: Alleviate pain and discomfort while antibiotics take effect

medicines.name: Phenazopyridine
medicines.dosage: 200 mg three times daily for maximum 2 days

trigger_avoidance: Wipe from front to back after toileting
recurrence_prevention: Topical vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal women

green_zone.action: Complete full antibiotic course; maintain hydration

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Supportive hydration and bladder-friendly diet aid symptom relief and recovery. No diet cures UTI, but adequate fluids promote bacterial flushing.

items.benefit: Increases urine volume to mechanically flush bacteria
Helps restore normal vaginal and gut flora disrupted by antibiotics

foods_to_avoid.food: Caffeine, Alcohol, Carbonated drinks, Spicy and Acidic Foods
foods_to_avoid.reason: These act as bladder irritants and can worsen dysuria and urgency

trigger_avoidance: Wipe from front to back after toileting
recurrence_prevention: Topical vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal women

key_points: All UTIs in pregnancy are considered complicated
Screen and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria to prevent pyelonephritis
Safe antibiotics include nitrofurantoin (avoid near term), beta-lactams, and fosfomycin
All male UTIs are considered complicated until proven otherwise
Evaluate for prostatitis or structural abnormalities

when_to_see_doctor: Symptoms not improving after 48 hours of treatment
Fever, flank pain, or systemic symptoms
emergency_signs: High fever with chills and flank pain
Severe vomiting or inability to tolerate fluids

faq.question: Can a UTI go away without antibiotics?
faq.answer: Some mild uncomplicated cases (25-42%) may resolve spontaneously, but antibiotics are recommended to shorten duration and prevent complications like pyelonephritis.

faq.question: How can recurrent UTIs be prevented?
faq.answer: Behavioral measures (post-coital voiding, hydration), D-mannose, vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal women, and probiotics are effective strategies.
